uk-documents-01.question: In England and Wales, the drink-drive limit is set as a breath measurement in law. What is the prescribed limit under s.11(2) Road Traffic Act 1988?

options.a: 22 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath
options.b: 35 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath
options.c: 50 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath
options.d: 80 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath

uk-documents-01.explanation: Under s.11(2) RTA 1988 the England & Wales limit is 35 µg of alcohol in 100 ml of breath (alongside 80 mg/100 ml blood and 107 mg/100 ml urine). This is roughly equivalent to 0.8‰ blood alcohol — noticeably higher than Germany's 0.5‰ limit (§ 24a StVG), or 0.0‰ for new drivers and those under 21. Unlike in Germany, the breath reading itself is the legally decisive evidential value in England and Wales, not just a preliminary screening test. Option a) is the lower Scottish limit (see the related question); c) and d) are invented intermediate figures.

uk-documents-02.question: Scotland has applied a stricter drink-drive limit than England and Wales since 2014. What is the breath limit under reg.2 of the Prescribed Limit (Scotland) Regulations 2014?

options.a: 22 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath
options.b: 35 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath
options.c: 45 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath
options.d: 0 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath (zero tolerance)

uk-documents-02.explanation: The Scottish Government lowered the limit in 2014 to 22 µg/100 ml breath (50 mg/100 ml blood, 67 mg/100 ml urine) — around 0.5‰ blood alcohol — while England and Wales remain at 35 µg/80 mg. UK road traffic law is therefore not uniform: driving in Glasgow means a stricter limit than in Manchester. Northern Ireland again has its own, entirely separate legislation. Germany applies a single nationwide limit of 0.5‰.

uk-documents-03.question: A driver is under the numeric alcohol limit but is clearly impaired by a strong sedative. What can they still be prosecuted for under the Road Traffic Act 1988?

options.a: Nothing, since no numeric limit was exceeded
options.b: Only a licensing matter under s.87
options.c: s.4: driving while unfit through drink or drugs, meaning the ability to drive properly is impaired
options.d: Only an insurance offence under s.143

uk-documents-03.explanation: s.4(1) and s.4(5) RTA 1988 turn on unfitness to drive — 'his ability to drive properly is for the time being impaired' — regardless of any numeric reading and regardless of whether the substance is alcohol, a prescribed medicine, or an illegal drug. This mirrors the underlying idea of § 316 StGB (driving while unfit), which also applies without a fixed limit where relative unfitness is shown through actual impairment.

uk-documents-04.question: For illegal drugs, s.5A Road Traffic Act 1988 sets a very strict approach in England and Wales. What is the specified limit for delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) under the Specified Limits Regulations 2014?

options.a: 500 micrograms per litre of blood, similar to methadone
options.b: 80 micrograms per litre of blood, similar to morphine
options.c: There is no limit at all — THC is excluded from s.5A
options.d: 2 micrograms per litre of blood — a very low, effectively strict limit

uk-documents-04.explanation: The s.5A regime introduced in 2014 sets very low limits for substances with no accepted medicinal use (e.g. THC: 2 µg/l, cocaine: 10 µg/l, LSD: 1 µg/l) — effectively zero tolerance. For medicines with legitimate use (e.g. diazepam: 550 µg/l, methadone: 500 µg/l) the limits sit far higher, paired with the prescribed-medicine defence in s.5A(3)-(5). Germany's § 24a(2) StVG also sets limits for controlled substances, but works with a single analytical threshold per substance rather than this two-tier recreational-drug/medicine logic.

uk-documents-05.question: A driver takes a strong painkiller exactly as prescribed by their doctor and is found over the s.5A limit for that substance. What does s.5A(3)-(5) Road Traffic Act 1988 provide?

options.a: They are automatically guilty; no defence is available
options.b: They can raise the prescribed-medicine defence if the drug was taken in accordance with medical and manufacturer instructions
options.c: The defence only applies if they are also under the alcohol limit
options.d: The defence only applies to holders of a provisional licence

uk-documents-05.explanation: s.5A(3) allows a defence where the drug was prescribed or supplied for medical purposes, taken in accordance with the prescriber's directions and the manufacturer's instructions, and possession was not otherwise unlawful. s.5A(4) defeats the defence if the driver ignored advice about the gap needed between taking the drug and driving; under s.5A(5) the defence is treated as made out unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that it is not. § 24a StVG has no equivalent statutory medicine defence framed this way.

uk-documents-06.question: What does s.87(1) Road Traffic Act 1988 require of anyone driving a motor vehicle on a road?

options.a: They must hold a licence authorising them to drive a vehicle of that class
options.b: They must additionally have signed a separate international driving permit agreement
options.c: Only insurance is required; a licence is not strictly necessary
options.d: They must be an adult holding at least a category B licence, regardless of the vehicle actually driven

uk-documents-06.explanation: s.87(1) makes it an offence to drive a motor vehicle otherwise than in accordance with a licence authorising that class; s.87(2) also catches someone who permits another to drive without the appropriate entitlement. As in Germany (§ 21 StVG, driving without a licence), what matters is the correct vehicle category, not merely holding some licence — a car licence does not automatically entitle someone to drive a lorry or motorcycle.

uk-documents-07.question: A learner is practising in a car on a provisional licence. What conditions must be met under reg.16 and reg.17 of the 1999 Regulations?

options.a: It is enough for any passenger over 17 to be in the car
options.b: No accompanying supervisor is needed as long as L-plates are displayed
options.c: L-plates must be displayed, and the supervisor must be at least 21 years old and have held the relevant full licence for at least 3 years
options.d: The supervisor must be a qualified, certified driving instructor — an ordinary licence holder is not enough

uk-documents-07.explanation: reg.16 requires visible L-plates front and back plus supervision by a 'qualified driver'; reg.17 defines that as at least 21 years old, having held the relevant full licence for at least 3 years (continuously or in aggregate) — an ordinary experienced driver qualifies, a certified instructor is not required. Germany's nearest equivalent, the supervisor for 'Begleitetes Fahren ab 17', must be at least 30 and have held the relevant licence for 5 years — a similar idea with different numbers, inside a different legal framework (Germany has no continuous provisional-licence system like the UK's).

uk-documents-08.question: From what vehicle age does s.47 Road Traffic Act 1988 generally require a valid test certificate (MOT) before the vehicle may be used on a road?

options.a: From 1 year old for all private cars
options.b: From 3 years old for most private motor vehicles (with a shorter period for, e.g., taxis and certain passenger-carrying vehicles)
options.c: From 10 years old, regardless of vehicle type
options.d: There is no age threshold — every vehicle needs an MOT from day one

uk-documents-08.explanation: s.47(1) makes it an offence to use a motor vehicle without a valid test certificate within the relevant period; for most private vehicles this duty starts 3 years after first registration, while certain passenger-carrying vehicles, licensed taxis and ambulances face a 1-year threshold. Germany's Hauptuntersuchung (HU) serves a similar function, also starting after 3 years for new cars, but then falls due every 2 years — whereas once due, the MOT is required annually.

uk-documents-09.question: What does s.143 Road Traffic Act 1988 require regarding motor insurance?

options.a: A person using a motor vehicle on a road or other public place must be covered by a policy of insurance meeting the statutory requirements against third-party risks — breach is an offence
options.b: Insurance is only compulsory for vehicles over 3.5 tonnes
options.c: The insurance duty falls only on the registered keeper, not on the actual driver
options.d: Fully comprehensive cover is a legal requirement

uk-documents-09.explanation: s.143(1) makes it an offence to use a motor vehicle without third-party insurance meeting the statutory requirements; s.143(3) provides a limited defence for an employee driving someone else's vehicle in the course of employment without knowing cover was missing. As under Germany's Pflichtversicherungsgesetz, third-party liability cover is the statutory minimum; comprehensive cover — contrary to option d) — is optional in both countries.

uk-documents-10.question: A vehicle is used or kept on a public road without vehicle excise duty being paid and a valid vehicle licence in force for it. What follows under s.29 Vehicle Excise and Registration Act 1994?

options.a: Nothing, as long as the vehicle is insured
options.b: Nothing, as long as the vehicle has a valid MOT
options.c: It is only a civil debt for back payment, not a criminal offence
options.d: It is an offence ('using or keeping an unlicensed vehicle'), unless an exemption applies, such as a valid SORN declaration

uk-documents-10.explanation: s.29 VERA 1994 makes it an offence to use or keep a vehicle without a vehicle licence or trade licence in force; exemptions include vehicles covered by a valid off-road declaration (SORN – Statutory Off Road Notification), since they are not used or kept on public roads. On conviction the penalty is the greater of level 3 on the standard scale or five times the vehicle excise duty chargeable. Germany's Kfz-Steuer is likewise a precondition tied to registration, but unlike in the UK it is not pursued as its own separate offence distinct from the registration process itself.

uk-priority-01.question: At a T-junction marked with a broken white give-way line and the Give Way sign (inverted triangle), what does TSRGD 2016 require of the driver?

options.a: Always stop completely, even if the road is clear
options.b: Not cross the line in a way that endangers a vehicle on the major road or forces it to change speed or course
options.c: Give way only to vehicles turning right
options.d: Apply a general 'priority to the right' rule as at an unmarked German junction

uk-priority-01.explanation: Under TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 7, paragraph 3, a vehicle must not cross the give-way line so as to endanger a vehicle on the major road or force it to change speed or course. Unlike Germany's default 'priority to the right' (rechts vor links) at unmarked junctions, the UK has almost no unmarked junctions of that kind - nearly every junction carries a Give Way, Stop, or priority sign or marking. Note: Northern Ireland has its own, separate regulations.

uk-priority-02.question: At a junction with the red octagonal STOP sign and a solid white stop line, TSRGD 2016 requires the driver to...

options.a: Slow down and proceed if clear, as at a give-way line
options.b: Stop completely before the line, even if no traffic is visible on the major road
options.c: Stop only if a pedestrian is waiting
options.d: Give way only to vehicles from the right

uk-priority-02.explanation: TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 7, paragraph 1 requires a full stop at the line regardless of visible traffic, unlike the broken give-way line, where stopping is only required if necessary. This mirrors the German distinction between a Stopschild and a Vorfahrt-gewähren sign, but is easy to get wrong if unfamiliar with UK signage.

uk-priority-03.question: At a UK roundabout, TSRGD 2016 requires an entering driver to give way at the give-way line to...

options.a: vehicles already circulating on the roundabout, coming from the right, since traffic drives on the left and circulates clockwise
options.b: vehicles coming from the left, as on a mainland-European roundabout
options.c: no one - entering traffic always has priority
options.d: buses and emergency vehicles only

uk-priority-03.explanation: Diagram 1003.3 (TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 6, item 6, read with Part 7, paragraph 7) requires an entering vehicle to give way to traffic already circulating. Because the UK drives on the left, roundabouts rotate clockwise and priority comes from the right - the mirror image of a German driver's instinct, where roundabouts rotate anticlockwise and priority comes from the left.

uk-priority-04.question: A yellow box junction (crossed yellow grid lines) under TSRGD 2016 means a vehicle must not enter it unless...

options.a: its exit road or lane is clear, so it will not have to stop within the yellow grid
options.b: the signal is green, regardless of the queue ahead
options.c: it is being used exclusively by buses
options.d: there is no other vehicle anywhere at the junction

uk-priority-04.explanation: TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 7, paragraph 10 prohibits entering a box junction if the vehicle would have to stop within it because of stationary vehicles. There is no direct German equivalent; the closest concept is the general duty not to block a junction when traffic is backed up (StVO section 11(1)), but the marked yellow grid as its own traffic sign is a UK-specific device.

uk-priority-05.question: A driver is waiting inside a yellow box junction to turn right. Under TSRGD 2016, this is permitted when the driver is...

options.a: prevented from completing the turn only by oncoming traffic, or by other vehicles waiting to turn right
options.b: never permitted to do so - the only exception is for emergency vehicles
options.c: signalling right at any time
options.d: waiting there only outside peak traffic hours

uk-priority-05.explanation: TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 7, paragraph 10 carves out an explicit exception for right turns: a driver prevented from clearing the box only by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right may wait inside it. This nuance is widely missed - option (b) states the common but incorrect belief that the prohibition is absolute.

uk-priority-06.question: The 'priority to right' sign/marking (diagram 1003.4) under TSRGD 2016 requires a driver entering the junction to...

options.a: give way to vehicles from the right - similar to Germany's unsigned 'priority to the right' rule, but here it applies only where this specific sign is actually posted
options.b: give way to vehicles from the left, as at an ordinary UK roundabout
options.c: always have priority regardless of other traffic
options.d: treat the junction as a mini-roundabout

uk-priority-06.explanation: TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 7, paragraph 5 requires priority from the right at this rare sign - the one UK situation that genuinely resembles the German default of 'priority to the right'. The key difference: in Germany this applies unsigned as the default rule for equal-ranking roads, whereas in the UK this specific sign must actually be erected, or the rule does not apply.

uk-priority-07.question: At a UK mini-roundabout (a flat painted white circle with no raised island, diagram 1003.3), a driver must give way under TSRGD 2016 to...

options.a: traffic already circulating, coming from the right - exactly as at a full-size roundabout
options.b: no one, since a marking with no physical island carries no priority rule
options.c: only larger vehicles unable to steer around the marking
options.d: pedestrians only

uk-priority-07.explanation: Diagram 1003.3, per TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 6, item 6, expressly covers 'a roundabout with a small central island' - i.e. the mini-roundabout. The give-way-to-the-right rule is identical to a full-size roundabout; only the physical form differs, which often tempts learners into the wrong assumption in option (b).

uk-priority-08.question: A driver ignores a lawfully placed STOP or Give Way sign. Under the Road Traffic Act 1988...

options.a: the driver commits an offence under section 36 for failing to comply with the indication given by the sign
options.b: the driver is only liable if a collision actually results
options.c: this is only an offence for a STOP sign, not for a Give Way sign
options.d: this only breaches a non-binding recommendation, like Highway Code guidance

uk-priority-08.explanation: Section 36 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 makes it an offence to fail to comply with the indication given by a properly authorised traffic sign - this applies equally to STOP and Give Way signs. Unlike much general advice in the Highway Code, which carries no legal force of its own, these 'MUST' rules rest on genuine statute.

uk-priority-09.question: A white direction arrow painted on the road at a junction or roundabout approach (e.g. 'must turn left', diagram 1036.1) is, under TSRGD 2016...

options.a: legally binding - a vehicle in that lane must follow the mandated direction, it is not merely a suggestion
options.b: purely advisory, like a non-binding lane-use hint
options.c: binding only for buses and lorries
options.d: safe to ignore as long as the correct indicator is used

uk-priority-09.explanation: The arrow (diagram 1036.1, TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 6, item 19) is a prescribed traffic sign; a driver in that lane must follow it, and disobeying it is an offence under section 36 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 - comparable to the German mandatory lane arrow (Zeichen 297 StVO), which is likewise binding rather than merely advisory.

uk-priority-10.question: Where a cycle track crosses a side road and carries the cyclists' give-way marking (diagram 1003B, the 'elephant's footprints'), TSRGD 2016 requires the cyclist there to...

options.a: give way to traffic on the road being crossed, just as a driver must at an ordinary give-way line
options.b: always have priority over turning traffic, regardless of the marking
options.c: dismount and push the bicycle across
options.d: is not covered by any traffic sign regulation

uk-priority-10.explanation: TSRGD 2016, Schedule 9, Part 7, paragraph 8 requires a cyclist at this marking to give way to the road. This is the point of contrast with German expectations: a cyclist on a physically separated track running alongside a priority road often keeps priority when crossing a minor side road (StVO section 9(3)); in the UK it depends entirely on which marking is actually installed - here a give-way marking, so the road has priority.

uk-signs-01.question: Under the UK traffic sign regulations (TSRGD 2016), a warning of a hazard ahead (for example a bend or a junction) must be conveyed by a sign of which shape?

options.a: Triangular
options.b: Circular
options.c: Octagonal
options.d: Rectangular

uk-signs-01.explanation: TSRGD 2016 Schedule 2 Part 1 paragraph 1 requires warning signs to be triangular (white or yellow background, red border) - the same convention used in Germany, so this one is a familiar shape, not a trap.

uk-signs-02.question: In Great Britain, which shape conveys a mandatory or prohibitory requirement for moving traffic (for example "turn left" or "no entry")?

options.a: Circular
options.b: Triangular
options.c: Rectangular
options.d: Diamond-shaped

uk-signs-02.explanation: TSRGD 2016 Schedule 3 Part 1 paragraph 1 requires circular signs for mandatory/prohibitory requirements on moving traffic - matching the German convention of round mandatory/prohibitory signs. Rectangles are reserved for informatory plates in both systems.

uk-signs-03.question: At a junction with a sign to diagram 601.1 (STOP) in Great Britain, TSRGD 2016 requires a vehicle to:

options.a: always come to a complete stop before the transverse stop line, even if the major road is clearly clear
options.b: stop only if another vehicle is approaching
options.c: stop only after dark
options.d: merely slow down, as with a give-way sign

uk-signs-03.explanation: Schedule 9 Part 7 paragraph 1 requires a complete stop at the line regardless of whether the road looks clear - unlike the give-way sign (diagram 602), which only requires stopping "if necessary". This matches the German Stopp-Schild (Zeichen 206) exactly, so no contrast here.

uk-signs-04.question: What order of illumination does TSRGD 2016 prescribe for a standard UK traffic light signal?

options.a: Red - red and amber together - green - amber
options.b: Red - green - amber (no red-and-amber phase)
options.c: Red - amber - green
options.d: Green - amber - red - straight back to green

uk-signs-04.explanation: Schedule 14 Part 1 paragraph 5 prescribes exactly the sequence red, red-and-amber, green, amber - the same "get ready" red-and-amber phase that German traffic lights also use. That is not universal: many countries (the USA, for instance) go straight from red to green with no warning phase at all.

uk-signs-05.question: When red and amber are shown together at a UK traffic light, TSRGD 2016 requires a vehicle to:

options.a: still wait at the stop line - it carries the same prohibition as red alone, and only signals that green is about to appear
options.b: proceed, as if it were green
options.c: proceed only if turning left
options.d: stop even if it has already crossed the stop line

uk-signs-05.explanation: Schedule 14 Part 1 paragraph 5 makes clear that red and amber together carry the same prohibition as red alone, merely warning that green is imminent. This matches the German red-and-amber phase exactly - one of the rare cases where UK and German law behave identically.

uk-signs-06.question: An amber signal shown alone at a UK traffic light means a driver must stop, EXCEPT when:

options.a: the vehicle is already so close to the stop line that stopping abruptly would be dangerous, in which case it may proceed
options.b: the vehicle is turning left, in which case amber may always be treated as green
options.c: it is dark, when amber alone does not apply
options.d: the vehicle is a bus or emergency vehicle, which may always disregard amber

uk-signs-06.explanation: Schedule 14 Part 1 paragraph 5 only allows proceeding on amber alone when it is no longer possible to stop safely before the line - which lands on the same result as the German amber rule: stop, unless stopping can no longer be done safely.

uk-signs-07.question: On a stretch of road marked with double white lines, TSRGD 2016 primarily prohibits - subject to a few exceptions such as loading/unloading or picking up/setting down passengers -:

options.a: stopping on that stretch of road
options.b: driving faster than 30 mph
options.c: driving without dipped headlights
options.d: cyclists using that stretch of road

uk-signs-07.explanation: Schedule 9 Part 7 paragraph 9(1)-(4) bans stopping on a length of road marked this way, with narrow exceptions (loading/unloading, picking up or setting down passengers, emergencies, certain vehicles). That is a stricter effect than a plain German continuous centre line, which by itself carries no stopping ban.

uk-signs-08.question: Where the continuous line of a double white line marking is on your side, TSRGD 2016 permits crossing it, among other things, to:

options.a: pass a stationary vehicle, turn into or out of a property or side road, or overtake a road maintenance vehicle travelling under 10 mph, where it is safe to do so
options.b: overtake generally, whenever the opposite carriageway looks clear
options.c: make a U-turn whenever no other vehicles are visible
options.d: exceed the applicable speed limit

uk-signs-08.explanation: Schedule 9 Part 7 paragraph 9(5) lists narrowly defined exceptions for crossing the continuous line. There is no general right to overtake just because the other carriageway looks clear - which is the assumption a German driver, used to a simple no-overtaking marking, might wrongly make.

uk-signs-09.question: A double yellow line (diagram 1018.1) along the edge of the carriageway in Great Britain means waiting is prohibited:

options.a: at all times, regardless of any nearby plate
options.b: only during the hours shown on a nearby plate
options.c: only on weekdays
options.d: only where a separate circular prohibition sign is also present

uk-signs-09.explanation: TSRGD 2016 Schedule 7 Part 4 assigns diagram 1018.1 (double yellow line) a waiting prohibition that applies at all times; the single yellow line (diagram 1017) instead marks a prohibition for specific times, usually given on a nearby plate. A German restricted no-waiting sign with a time plate is closer to the single yellow line than to the double.

uk-signs-10.question: On a "red route" (mainly found in London), a sign under TSRGD 2016 Schedule 6 may show, in its lower panel, exceptions to the stopping restriction for:

options.a: buses, taxis, ambulances and police vehicles
options.b: emergency vehicles only
options.c: any vehicle displaying a disabled badge, without further limit
options.d: no vehicles at all - red route signs allow no exception under the regulations

uk-signs-10.explanation: TSRGD 2016 Schedule 6 provides for "RED ROUTE" signs with a middle panel giving times and possible exceptions (including buses, taxis, ambulances, police vehicles, "BUS STAND"). Red routes rest on traffic orders made under the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 and are mainly an English (London) scheme - Scotland, Wales, and especially Northern Ireland (its own separate legislation) do not have an identical arrangement.

uk-speed-01.question: A plain white circular sign with a black diagonal bar stands at the roadside. What does it mean?

options.a: There is no speed limit from here on, like the German 'end of all restrictions' sign.
options.b: The national speed limit applies from here for this type of road and this vehicle.
options.c: Overtaking is prohibited from here.
options.d: A motorway begins here.

uk-speed-01.explanation: The numberless sign (TSRGD 2016, Schedule 10, diagram 671) simply switches on whichever national speed limit applies to that road type and vehicle class – e.g. 60 mph on a single carriageway or 70 mph on a motorway/dual carriageway for a car. It does not mean 'no limit', unlike the German sign that genuinely lifts all limits on the Autobahn.

uk-speed-02.question: On a 'restricted road' in England and Wales (broadly: a road with street lighting) with no numbered sign, what speed limit applies by law?

options.a: 50 mph, matching a built-up-area limit in Germany once converted.
options.b: 40 mph.
options.c: 30 mph.
options.d: 20 mph.

uk-speed-02.explanation: Section 81 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 sets the default limit on 'restricted roads' at 30 mph (about 48 km/h) without any numbered sign being needed – the street lighting itself signals the restriction. The German equivalent, 50 km/h in built-up areas, is announced by the town-name sign; the English figure is lower.

uk-speed-03.question: A car is on a single-carriageway road outside a restricted area, with no numbered sign, so the 'national speed limit' applies. What is its maximum speed?

options.a: 70 mph.
options.b: 60 mph.
options.c: 50 mph.
options.d: 80 mph.

uk-speed-03.explanation: Under s.86 and Schedule 6 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984, the national speed limit for a car on a single carriageway is 60 mph (about 97 km/h) – lower than on a motorway or dual carriageway. A German driver thinking of the 100 km/h Landstraße guideline would be driving too fast here.

uk-speed-04.question: A car is on a motorway or a dual carriageway with no numbered sign. What speed limit applies to it by law, regardless of how good the road is?

options.a: 70 mph, whatever the conditions.
options.b: No limit, provided the weather is good.
options.c: 130 mph as a mere advisory speed.
options.d: 80 mph.

uk-speed-04.explanation: Schedule 6 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 caps cars on motorways and dual carriageways at 70 mph (about 113 km/h) – a hard limit, not a guideline. This is fundamentally different from the German Autobahn, which often has only an advisory 130 km/h speed with no binding general limit.

uk-speed-05.question: A car is towing a caravan on a motorway. What maximum speed applies to that combination?

options.a: 70 mph, the same as without a trailer.
options.b: 50 mph.
options.c: 60 mph.
options.d: 40 mph.

uk-speed-05.explanation: Schedule 6 lowers the limit for a car towing a trailer or caravan to 60 mph on motorways and dual carriageways, and to 50 mph on single carriageways. In Germany a suitably certified combination with a 'Tempo 100' permit may go as fast as 100 km/h – there is no equivalent exception in Great Britain.

uk-speed-06.question: A goods vehicle with a maximum laden weight over 7.5 tonnes is on a single-carriageway road. What speed limit applies to it?

options.a: 60 mph, the same as on a motorway.
options.b: 50 mph.
options.c: 40 mph.
options.d: 70 mph, the same as a car on a motorway.

uk-speed-06.explanation: Schedule 6 sets the limit for goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes at 50 mph (about 80 km/h) on single carriageways, against 60 mph on motorways and dual carriageways. German lorries are also capped at 80 km/h on the Autobahn, but the British system tiers the limit more finely by road type.

uk-speed-07.question: On a motorway with three through lanes running the same direction, a goods vehicle over 7.5 tonnes wants to move into the outermost right-hand lane to overtake. Is that allowed?

options.a: No – that lorry is barred from the right-hand lane altogether, even to overtake.
options.b: Yes, exactly like any other vehicle.
options.c: Yes, but only at night.
options.d: Yes, as long as it stays under 60 mph while there.

uk-speed-07.explanation: Regulation 12 of the Motorways Traffic (England and Wales) Regulations 1982 bars goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes, buses/coaches over 12 metres long, and vehicles towing trailers from the right-hand lane whenever a carriageway has three or more through lanes – overtaking or not. German law has stretch-specific lorry overtaking bans, but no blanket ban on lorries using the outermost lane itself.

uk-speed-08.question: May a learner driver on a provisional licence drive on a motorway in Great Britain?

options.a: Yes, without restriction, once they turn 17.
options.b: No, never before passing the driving test.
options.c: Only in a dual-controlled car, supervised by an approved driving instructor.
options.d: Yes, supervised by any driver with at least three years' experience, as for ordinary practice drives.

uk-speed-08.explanation: Regulation 11 used to bar learners from motorways entirely. Since a 2018 amendment they may practise there, but only in a car fitted with dual controls (clutch and brake operable independently) and supervised by a registered approved driving instructor – not by any experienced passenger, as suffices for ordinary learner practice.

uk-speed-09.question: Which of the following are generally NOT allowed to use a British motorway?

options.a: Coaches.
options.b: Motorcycles of 125cc or more.
options.c: Goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes.
options.d: Pedestrians, pedal cyclists, and vehicles under 50cc engine capacity.

uk-speed-09.explanation: Regulation 15 permits motorways only to 'traffic of Classes I or II' under Schedule 4 to the Highways Act 1980; excluded traffic includes pedestrians, pedal cycles, motorcycles under 50cc, pedestrian-controlled vehicles, animal-drawn vehicles and invalid carriages. Unlike German Autobahnen, which simply require vehicles capable of a minimum design speed, British law lists the excluded classes in fine, itemised detail.

uk-speed-10.question: A driver wants to make a brief stop on a motorway's hard shoulder to check a map. Is that allowed?

options.a: Yes, for up to 15 minutes.
options.b: No – the hard shoulder may only be used for a breakdown, accident or other emergency.
options.c: Yes, provided the hazard lights are on.
options.d: Yes, anywhere along the route without restriction.

uk-speed-10.explanation: Regulation 9 bans driving or stopping on the hard shoulder outright; Regulation 7(2) allows exceptions only for breakdown, accident, running out of fuel, or a similar emergency. On so-called 'smart motorways' the hard shoulder can also serve as an ordinary running lane, but only when overhead signs expressly show it is open (Regulation 16) – a red 'X' still means it is closed. A casual stop just to check a map is never permitted, unlike habits some drivers bring from the German hard shoulder (Seitenstreifen).

uk-vulnerable-01.question: A pedestrian is already on the carriageway within the limits of a Zebra crossing before any part of a vehicle has entered those limits. What does UK law say?

options.a: The pedestrian only has precedence if they visibly signal an intention to cross, as under German law.
options.b: The pedestrian has precedence over every vehicle within the limits of the crossing.
options.c: Vehicles have precedence provided they are already moving.
options.d: Precedence only applies between 7am and 7pm.

uk-vulnerable-01.explanation: Regulation 25 of the 1997 Regulations gives a pedestrian already within the crossing's limits unconditional precedence over any vehicle. German law (StVO s.26) instead requires the pedestrian to make their intention to cross clearly apparent before precedence arises – a subtle but exam-relevant difference.

uk-vulnerable-02.question: What does regulation 20 of the 1997 Regulations say about the 'controlled area' (the zigzag lines before and after a crossing)?

options.a: Parking is allowed there whenever hazard lights are on.
options.b: The zigzag markings are purely advisory with no legal effect.
options.c: The driver must not cause the vehicle to stop there, subject to limited exceptions.
options.d: Only lorries may stop there.

uk-vulnerable-02.explanation: Regulation 20 prohibits a driver from causing a vehicle to stop within the controlled area (zigzag markings), subject to the exceptions in regulations 21 and 22. Germany has no equivalent zigzag no-stopping zone before a Zebrastreifen; there the general rule is StVO s.12 (no stopping within 5m before a pedestrian crossing).

uk-vulnerable-03.question: A driver approaching a Zebra crossing within the controlled area wants to overtake another, slower vehicle. What applies?

options.a: They must not pass ahead of the foremost part of that other vehicle while within the controlled area.
options.b: Overtaking is allowed as long as speed stays under 30 mph.
options.c: Overtaking is only banned where there is a solid centre line, otherwise it is permitted.
options.d: The overtaking ban only applies to lorries over 3.5 tonnes.

uk-vulnerable-03.explanation: Regulation 24 bans overtaking ('passing ahead of the foremost part' of another vehicle) within the controlled area approaching a crossing, regardless of speed or vehicle class. German StVO s.26(3) similarly bans overtaking immediately before a pedestrian crossing, but without the UK's specific zigzag-zone definition.

uk-vulnerable-04.question: At a Pelican crossing, the vehicular light signal changes from red to flashing amber. Who has precedence if a pedestrian is already on the crossing?

options.a: The driver, because in Germany a flashing amber means 'proceed with caution'.
options.b: Neither – both must wait until green appears.
options.c: Ordinary priority-to-the-right applies.
options.d: The pedestrian, provided they were already on the crossing before any vehicle entered it.

uk-vulnerable-04.explanation: Regulation 26 gives the pedestrian precedence during the flashing-amber phase of a Pelican crossing, provided they entered the crossing before the vehicle did. German traffic-light-controlled pedestrian crossings have no equivalent flashing-amber phase for drivers; the signal simply switches straight between green and red.

uk-vulnerable-05.question: What is the key difference between a Puffin crossing and a Pelican crossing?

options.a: A Puffin crossing has no vehicular light signals at all.
options.b: A Puffin crossing has no flashing-amber phase; on-crossing detectors sense whether pedestrians remain and hold the vehicular signal at red accordingly.
options.c: A Puffin crossing is reserved exclusively for cyclists.
options.d: A Puffin crossing may only be installed outside built-up areas.

uk-vulnerable-05.explanation: Regulation 13 governs the vehicular light signals at a Puffin crossing: unlike the Pelican crossing (regulation 12), there is no flashing-amber phase; instead the signal stays red for as long as detectors sense pedestrians still on the crossing. This is unfamiliar to a German driver, since German pedestrian signals have no sensor-extended red phase of this kind.

uk-vulnerable-06.question: A School Crossing Patrol officer in prescribed uniform holds up a 'Stop – Children Crossing' sign while a schoolchild wants to cross. What is the legal effect under s.28 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984?

options.a: The sign is a mere recommendation carrying no offence, comparable to the German 'Schülerlotse' symbol.
options.b: The driver must only stop if directly addressed by the patrol.
options.c: The driver must stop before reaching the crossing point and must not move off again while the sign is displayed; failing to comply is an offence.
options.d: The duty only applies to vehicles over 3.5 tonnes.

uk-vulnerable-06.explanation: Section 28 makes stopping for a duly authorised School Crossing Patrol officer compulsory and makes non-compliance an offence. In Germany, the 'Schülerlotse' has no equivalent independent statutory power to compel drivers to stop; they operate purely through warning signals and the general duty of care.

uk-vulnerable-07.question: A driver enters a mandatory cycle lane marked with a solid white line (Diagram 1049 under TSRGD 2016) in order to park. Which provision makes this an offence?

options.a: Non-compliance is only a local parking matter with no criminal effect.
options.b: s.36 Road Traffic Act 1988 – failing to comply with a prescribed traffic sign is an offence.
options.c: Only German road traffic licensing rules (StVZO) are relevant here.
options.d: There is no sanction as long as no cyclist is actually obstructed.

uk-vulnerable-07.explanation: s.36 RTA 1988 makes it an offence to fail to comply with a lawfully placed traffic sign, including the marking of a mandatory cycle lane. In Germany a cycle path marked by sign 237 is likewise mandatory, and driving on it is a fineable offence under StVO s.49 – the structure is similar, but the legal basis is entirely different.

uk-vulnerable-08.question: At a shared crossing facility with dedicated cyclist light signals under Schedule 14 of the Traffic Signs Regulations and General Directions 2016 (commonly called a 'toucan crossing'), cyclists:

options.a: May ride across the carriageway without dismounting once the cyclist light signal permits it.
options.b: Must always dismount and push the bicycle across, as at a German pedestrian crossing.
options.c: Are generally prohibited from crossing at all.
options.d: Are governed by the same signal as pedestrians, with no separate cyclist signal.

uk-vulnerable-08.explanation: Schedule 14 provides for a dedicated cyclist light signal at crossing facilities shared with pedestrians, so cyclists may ride across without dismounting once it shows green. In Germany, cyclists must generally dismount at a Fußgängerüberweg (zebra crossing), since it is legally reserved for those on foot.

uk-vulnerable-09.question: At a level crossing the red light signal is showing. Which provision makes it an offence for a driver to cross against it?

options.a: The Level Crossings Act 1983 alone governs all sanctions against drivers.
options.b: There is no dedicated sanction; only the general duty of care applies.
options.c: s.36 Road Traffic Act 1988 – failing to comply with a prescribed traffic sign (here, the level crossing's red light signal) is an offence.
options.d: Only the railway operator can pursue the matter under private law.

uk-vulnerable-09.explanation: s.36 RTA 1988 generally covers failure to comply with lawfully placed traffic signs and light signals, which includes the red flashing lights at a level crossing. German law sanctions crossing against a red light at a level crossing under StVO s.19 in conjunction with the fine catalogue, but under a structurally different provision.

uk-vulnerable-10.question: A rider leads their horse across a Zebra crossing. Do they benefit from the precedence regulation 25 grants to 'every pedestrian'?

options.a: Yes, riders are expressly equated with pedestrians in the text.
options.b: Yes, but only if the horse is being led at walking pace.
options.c: No, because horses count as 'vehicles' under the Regulations.
options.d: No, regulation 25 expressly speaks of 'pedestrian'; a rider or their horse is not covered by that term.

uk-vulnerable-10.explanation: Regulation 25 grants precedence expressly to 'every pedestrian'; riders and horses are not covered by that wording and therefore have no statutory precedence at a Zebra crossing. Under German law, leading a horse across a Fußgängerüberweg is likewise not privileged by StVO s.26, since that provision covers only those on foot – in both systems, the rider is left without this specific protection.
